en: From the *Khecarīvidyā* of Ādinātha, edited by James Mallinson:
1.1ab Now, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the knowledge known as *khecarī*,
1.1cd by the realization of which one may become free from old age and death in this world.
1.2ab Having seen this entire universe seized by death, disease, and old age, O beloved,
1.2cd one should make one's intellect even firmer and take refuge in *khecarī*.
1.3ab He who knows *khecarī* on this earth [knows] that which destroys old age, death, and disease.

1.3cd Having bowed with one's whole being to that Guru, both in terms of the text and its meaning, and through the practice of that [teaching], 1.4ab one should take refuge in him, O Goddess; for the Khecarī-vidyā is difficult to obtain, and its practice is likewise difficult to attain. 1.4cd [The text continues: ...and its practice is difficult to obtain.
1.5ab Practice and the *melaka* do not succeed simultaneously.
1.5cd One who is intent on practice alone does not find the *melaka* in this world.
1.6ab O Goddess, through practice one may obtain it somewhere in another birth after many lifetimes.
1.6cd That meeting of those born [into this state] is not obtained even at the end of a hundred lifetimes. 1.7ab Having performed practice perfected through true being at the end of many births,
1.7cd O Goddess, the yogi obtains that meeting somewhere in another birth.
1.8ab But when the seeker of desire attains the *melaka*, O Supreme Goddess,
1.8cd then he obtains that accomplishment which has been described in the lineage of the scriptures.
1.9ab When he attains the *melaka* both in terms of the text and its meaning, [he achieves success].
1.9cd Then one attains the state of Śiva, liberated from the fear of saṃsāra.
1.10ab Even gurus would not be able to fully understand it without the scripture.
1.10cd Therefore, O beloved, this scripture is most difficult to obtain, yet once obtained, it is [of supreme value].
1.11ab As long as this text is not obtained, one should wander this earth.
1.11cd O Goddess, when it is obtained, then accomplishment (siddhi) rests in the palm of one's hand.
1.12ab Without the scripture, there is no accomplishment even for one wandering through the three worlds.

"Therefore, O Īśvarī, one should always worship the giver of the *melaka*, the giver of the scripture, and the giver of its practice, regarding them as Śiva himself. And many tantras have been proclaimed by me, O Goddess worshipped by the gods."
1.14ab In those [places], the khecarī-siddhi that destroys death is not proclaimed.
1.14cd [The sites are] Mahākāla, Mārtaṇḍa, Vivekādyam, and Śābara;
1.15ab [the site] known as Viśuddheśvara, and likewise Jālaśaṃvara.
1.15cd In these excellent tantras, that practice has been revealed;
1.16ab in some places it is clear, in others unclear, such as the *melaka* and so forth.
1.16cd In this divine, supreme tantra, the *melaka* and other [practices] have been fully disclosed.
1.17ab Whatever may be known, and whatever is difficult to know according to the Khecarī doctrine, 1.17cd all that has been revealed here by us out of affection for you.
1.18ab Therefore, let this wonderful scripture spoken by me be acquired.
1.18cd O Great Goddess, this must be kept secret; it has not been revealed everywhere.
1.19ab He who speaks the nectar of the scriptures born from the lotus of my mouth— 1.19cd he alone is truly the Guru, for he understands the meaning in its true sense.
1.20ab And he is known as the most eminent teacher; there is no one superior to him. 1.20cd Having obtained this secret scripture, one should not reveal it to others.
1.21ab This should be taught only after careful consideration to those who subsist upon this path.
1.21cd Whoever should reveal this supreme scripture here or there,
1.22ab he shall quickly be devoured, O Goddess, by the Yoginīs at the command of Śiva. 1.22cd One should not untie its knot without the satiation of the Kaulikas.
1.23ab Honored, placed within a beautiful cloth, and well-perfumed with divine incense;
1.23cd one should cause it to be heard by a yogin endowed with yoga in a secluded place. 1.24ab In whichever house this scripture remains unhonored, indeed—
1.24cd There, it is certain that affliction from fire, disease, planets, and enemies shall arise.
1.25ab O Pārvatī, in whatever house this honored text remains,
1.25cd there the family deities (kuladevatās), who bestow all desired objects, reside.
Therefore, one who understands this should guard it with every effort. But that yogi who desires these perfections (siddhis) which have been described by me—
such a yogi should guard this book with his whole being.

1.27cd O Goddess, I am his guru wherever the book itself resides. 1.28ab O Maheśānī, by virtue of protecting the book, its merits and defects have been clearly explained by me; now listen to the Khecarī.
1.29ab Wherever the Guru resides, O Goddess, who accomplishes divine yoga,
1.29cd one should go there and receive from him the *vidyā* of the *khecarī*. 1.30ab One should first perform the practice correctly and without sloth, as instructed by him.
1.30cd O Goddess, I shall now proclaim the *vidyā* known as Khecarī, which bestows the perfection of yoga.

1.31ab A yogi who is devoid of it cannot become a partaker of the perfection of Khecarī. 1.31cd By uniting Khecarī with Khecarī, preceded by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Khecarī, [one attains success].

Having become the lord of the sky-dwellers (khecaras), one shall dwell forever among the sky-dwellers. The fire that is the abode of the sky-dwellers, adorned by the circle of the Mother (Ambā), is explained as the seed-syllable (bīja) of Khecarī; through it, yoga is perfected.
1.33cd The one called *Mastaka* is Mahācaṇḍā, who bears the peacock, fire, and the thunderbolt.
1.34ab This Vidyā, joined with the initial seed-syllable, is indeed explained as being extremely difficult to obtain.
1.34cd I shall now describe the six-limbed Vidyā, which is differentiated by those six vowels.
1.35ab O Goddess, one should perform [this] according to the rule for the sake of attaining all accomplishments (siddhi).
1.35cd One should extract the ninth letter from Soma and Īśāna in reverse order. 1.36ab Therefore, it is called the thirtieth syllable, which has the form of the Moon.
1.36cd–1.37ab: From that [eighth vowel] as well, O Dear One, the other eighth syllable in reverse order;
likewise, O Goddess, its fifth, and the fifth beginning with that [fifth]. 1.37cd: Even Indra (the letter *i*) conjoined with the Bindu—this is proclaimed as the *kūṭa*.

1.39cd He who recites these five hundred thousand [mantras], being extremely well-restrained,
1.40ab for him the accomplishment of Śrī Khecarī proceeds of its own accord;
1.40cd all obstacles perish and the deities become propitious.
1.41ab There will be the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair; of this there is no doubt.
1.41cd Having thus obtained the Great Vidyā, one should then perform its practice.
1.42ab Otherwise, O Goddess, one suffers; there is no accomplishment in the state of Khecarī.

1.42cd If one does not obtain the nectar-like knowledge during the rite of practice, 1.43ab then, having obtained the knowledge at the time of the *saṃmelaka* and so forth, one should recite it thoroughly. 1.43cd O Goddess, deprived of this, one shall never partake in success (*siddhi*).
1.44ab When this scripture is obtained, then one should take recourse in the knowledge (vidyā).
1.44cd Thereupon, O beloved, one quickly attains the accomplishment (siddhi) proclaimed therein.
1.45ab Having extracted [the syllable] from the root of the palate for seven days, the knower of the self—

1.45cd One should purify all impurities according to the method taught by one's own guru. 1.46ab Having taken up a very sharp instrument that resembles a snuhī leaf, being smooth and stainless, 1.46cd one should then excise [the hair] to the thickness of a single hair with it.
Having cut [the hair], one should rub [the area] with powdered rock salt (saindhava) and Pathyā.
When seven days have passed again, one should shave it down to the length of a single hair.
In this manner, one should practice diligently every day for six months.
1.48cd Within six months, the binding of the channels at the root of the tongue perishes. 1.49ab Alternatively, the head—the abode of Vāgīśvarī—is wrapped in a cloth;
1.49cd the yogi, knowing the rules for the timing of the practice, should gradually draw it upward.
Furthermore, O Dear One, by constant practice for just six months,
it reaches as far as the middle of the eyebrows, extending horizontally to the openings of the ears;
and through gradual application, it moves downward to the root of the chin.
Furthermore, O Dear One, from the very third year onwards, by way of play,
it moves upward to the hairline and transversely as far as the temples;
then, after another three years, it reaches down to the pit of the throat.
O Goddess worshipped by the immortals, it remains pervading as far as the *brahmarandhra*;
it extends obliquely to the surface of the crown of the head and downwards as far as the cavity of the throat.
One should practice this very gradually; certainly not all at once.
1.54cd For one who should practice [this] simultaneously, his body would go to destruction.
1.55ab Therefore, O fair-complexioned lady, the practice should be performed very gradually.
1.55cd And when the tongue reaches the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila) by way of the external path...
1.56ab Then, O Goddess, the bolt of Brahmā, which is difficult even for the gods to break, [is opened].
1.56cd Rubbing [the tongue] with the tip of the finger, one should place the tongue there.
1.57ab Having practiced thus for three years, one enters the gate of Brahmā.
1.57cd But once [the breath] has entered the Gate of Brahman (brahmadvāra), one should properly begin the churning (mathana). 1.58ab Some wise ones accomplish [the goal] without churning.
1.58cd For one who has attained mastery over the Khecarī-mantra, success is achieved even without churning.
Having performed both the recitation (*japa*) and the churning (*mathana*), one shall quickly obtain the fruit.
Having inserted a probe made of gold, silver, or even iron into the nostril with a firm and smooth thread—
1.60cd Having firmly established his seat with the vital breaths restrained in the heart,
1.61ab he should perform churning slowly, fixing his eyes between the eyebrows;
1.61cd the state of churning arises after six months, and by that much alone.
1.62ab For the yogin whose vital breath is perfectly restrained and whose self is absorbed in that [state], 1.62cd his state at that time becomes like the deep sleep of children.
1.63ab Constant churning is not recommended; one should practice it month by month.
1.63cd O Goddess, one should always traverse the path with the tongue.
1.64ab Thus, at the end of twelve years, there is supreme accomplishment, O Parameśvarī.
1.64cd One perceives the entire universe within the body as non-different from oneself.
1.65ab One should know that the Trikūṭa, frequented by the Siddhas, is located within the Brahmāṇḍa on the great path, above the circle of the rājadanta (upper palate) and between the eyebrows.
1.65cd–66ab There, one should fix the mind upon that which resembles the sprout of a chickpea.
Licking with the tongue the supreme nectar flowing there,
O beloved, one who follows the path of gradual practice should drink it for four years; thus,
the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair occurs, and supreme perfection is attained.
1.68ab One who knows the meaning of all the scriptures shall live for a thousand years. 1.68cd The accomplishments (siddhis) such as mining, subterranean passages, alchemy of mercury, and so forth—
1.69ab these arise for the yogi within five years, O Pārvatī.
1.69cd–70ab. By drinking with his tongue the flowing water of nectar, the yogi, established in well-being and observing the vow, may live for twelve years.
1.70cd. Through this practice of yoga, he becomes free from wrinkles and grey hair.
1.71ab The great yogin with a vajra-body lives for a hundred thousand years.
1.71cd O Dear One, he is endowed with the strength of ten thousand elephants. 1.72ab He possesses the power of far-sight and likewise the power of hearing from afar.
1.72cd Capable of both restraint and favor, one becomes powerful in all respects.
1.73ab For these perfections, O Goddess, indeed arise within the space between the eyebrows.
1.73cd Having placed the tongue in the sky [of the palate], one should press against the row of teeth.
1.74ab Having formed his mouth like the beak of a crow, he should drink that nectar.
1.74cd By drinking it, after one year, he truly becomes free from old age and death. 1.75ab He attains the power of moving through the sky and lives as long as the moon and stars exist.
1.75cd Sandals, a sword, a vetāla, the substance of accomplishment, and realgar; 1.76ab collyrium, a subterranean opening, a servant, and likewise a yakṣiṇī—
whatever exists in the three worlds as a means for attaining supernatural powers (siddhi).
1.77ab The best of practitioners should accomplish all of that immediately.
2.1ab O Maheśvarī, where the door is barred by Brahmā and is difficult to discern,
2.1cd there resides the supreme quartet of *kalās*, which consists of the four aims of life.
2.2ab Named Kṛtā in the eastern part, Guptā in the southern region,
2.2cd Śivā in the western direction, and Parāparaśivā in the north;
2.3ab Having pierced that door with the tip of the tongue, one [attains] the nectar of the eastern digit.
2.3cd When the yogi indeed drinks [it], after one month he becomes the lord of dharma.
2.4ab When the yogi licks the secret nectar with his tongue on the right side,
2.4cd after just one month, without a doubt, he becomes the manifest lord of wealth.
2.5ab One should drink with the tongue that nectar produced from the western digit (kalā). 2.5cd When one does so, then after a month the great yogi becomes a Lord of Desire (Kāmeśvara).
2.6ab When one drinks the nectar produced from the northern digit (kalā),...

2.6cd Then he shall attain sovereignty over the Parameṣṭhin gods. 2.7ab When the supreme nectar, dissolved in the upper sphere, [reaches] the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), 2.7cd and when the lord of yogis drinks it, he becomes Śiva, liberated while living.
When one practices this for twelve years, with each month serving as the limit,
that yogi becomes free from all diseases, omniscient, and honored by sages; like Śiva, he is born in this world ageless and immortal.
2.9cd Having drunk again and again the four-part nectar-water, O Maheśvarī,
2.10ab one should likewise place the tongue in the station of Brahmā and drink the nectar—
2.10cd which is delicious, cool, pleasing to the heart, milk-colored, and free of froth.
2.11ab By practicing for only one month, one becomes like a god oneself.
2.11cd O Pārvatī, in two months, one correctly understands the meaning of all the scriptures.
2.12ab O Śivā, after three months, one indeed becomes independent like Śiva.
2.12cd O Maheśānī, after four months, omniscience arises.
2.13ab In the fifth month, the great adept beholds even the three worlds.
2.13cd In the sixth month, O Paramānanda, he is filled with the true existence of all qualities.
2.14ab There is no doubt that he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) in both the supreme and the non-supreme [realms].
2.14cd In the seventh month, he dwells constantly together with the great elements, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas,
2.15ab always in their company, with a joyful mind according to his own will.
2.15cd In the eighth month-cycle, there occurs a union with the gods.
2.16ab In the ninth month, invisibility and subtlety indeed arise.
2.16cd In the tenth month, there is the power of assuming any form at will, which illuminates all worlds.
2.17ab In the eleventh [birth], he becomes a lord and master who knows the three times and rules over all the worlds.
2.17cd O Goddess, he is born like Śiva; this which I have spoken is the truth.
2.18ab O Īśvarī, where the Cūlitala is proclaimed, they call that place Kedāra.
2.18cd Therein, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the eight digits of the Moon (somakalā) are renowned.
2.19ab The first, O Goddess, is Amṛtā; the second is named Mānadā. 2.19cd Then Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and likewise Dhṛti.
2.20ab All the [days] beginning with Śaśinī and ending with Aṣṭamī are great oceans of supreme nectar (parāmṛta).
2.20cd And when the yogi directs his tongue toward that abode,
2.21ab then a continuous stream of frost flows there eightfold.
2.21cd Through the union with that immersion, the decay of the body's diseases occurs;
2.22ab through eight cycles of months, the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) arises.
2.22cd That abode which is called the "middle of the eyebrows" is declared to be the lunar orb (*somamaṇḍala*).
2.23ab Therein, the group of four digits (kalās) is said to be the abode of supreme nectar (parāmṛta).
2.23cd They are known by the names Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, and Śrīś.
2.24ab Having inserted the tongue there, one should drink again and again until fully satiated.
2.24cd Within four months, the yogi becomes free from all afflictions.
2.25ab By drinking that [fluid] and bathing in it, one truly becomes possessed of a vajra-body.
2.25cd Above that is the stone known as the Vajrakanda, the mandala of the sky-farers.

2.26ab One should know that at the edge of the forehead, O Goddess, there are three digits (kalās). 2.26cd These are Prīti, Aṅgadā, and Pūrṇā; one should insert the tongue there. 2.27ab One should drink with the tongue the cool, flowing nectar of a stream of milk.

2.27cd O Goddess of gods, within three months one becomes free from all diseases. 2.28ab One becomes uncuttable by any weapons and unbreakable by any means. 2.28cd One becomes inconceivable even to those possessing all forms of specialized knowledge regarding the various sense objects.
2.29ab Through the power of the *vajrakanda*, one truly becomes like Bhairava.
2.29cd Below the nose and above the lower lip is the *rājadanta*; it is the great place (*mahāpada*).
2.30ab Therein, O Goddess, are the two digits (*kalā*): the Full Moon (*pūrṇāmṛtā*) and the Cool One (*śītalā*).
2.30cd Having attained the state of *kumbhaka*, one should touch [the palate] with the tip of the tongue.
2.31ab There, O Goddess, a delicious and cool water is produced.
2.31cd Joining one's own mind there, the observer of the vow should drink it for three months.
2.32ab One attains freedom from old age and death, being freed from all diseases. 2.32cd The location situated between the anus and the genitals is proclaimed as the *ādhāra*.
2.33ab Therein, five *kalās* are said to exist, dripping with the supreme nectar (*amṛta*).
2.33cd Nectar is wisdom consisting of nectar; it destroys time and bestows knowledge. 2.34ab The five digits (*kalās*) are proclaimed as streams of nectar that grant all accomplishments (*siddhis*).
2.34cd Residing therein is the supreme power, the primordial Kuṇḍalinī, O Śivā.
2.35ab Therein, O Goddess worshipped by the gods, by means of contraction through *kumbhaka* (retention),
2.35cd having reached the cool nectar situated there by means of the *mūla-śakti*,
2.36ab and having brought it up through the *suṣumṇā* from the lotuses of the *svādhiṣṭhāna* and the other centers,
2.36cd One should meditate upon that [universe] as being sprinkled by a rain of nectar, extending as far as the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
2.37ab There, the supreme Śakti, the illustrious Kuṇḍalinī, having taken up the nectar situated therein,
2.37cd and having reached the path of the Suṣumṇā, proceeds to the end of the abode of Brahman.
2.38ab One should meditate on [the goddess] born from the fivefold grain of the root-mantra, overflowing with the satisfaction of nectar.
2.38cd One should visualize her pervading the body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. 2.39ab Through the practice for five months, the dissolution of the five elements occurs.
2.39cd Through the yoga of practice throughout the three times, one truly becomes equal to Śiva.
2.40ab O Goddess, that which is the location of the *liṅga* is called the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. 2.40cd Therein, the three *kalās* consisting of divine nectar are said to reside.
2.41ab These are proclaimed as the Susūkṣmā, the Paramāhlādā, and the Vidyā [Kuṇḍalinīs].
2.41cd Having attained the state of kumbhaka as before and having awakened the Śakti,
2.42ab one should lead her to the limit of the Brahmāṇḍa and flood one's own body with it.
2.42cd After a period of three months, the yogi attains the fruit previously described. 2.43ab That which is between the anus and the genitals is called the "bamboo staff" (veṇudaṇḍa).
2.43cd It is said to consist of four digits (kalā) there, and its nature is the essence of supreme nectar.
2.44ab It is very cooling, provides great satisfaction, destroys gray hair, and diminishes wrinkles.
2.44cd Having awakened the *śakti* therein as before, one should bathe the body.
2.45ab By practicing this for four months, one obtains the results previously described.
2.45cd Piṅgalā is that which carries the sun; Iḍā is that which carries the moon.
2.46ab The sun is said to be the carrier of poison; the moon is the carrier of nectar.
2.46cd Practice is recommended during both the flow known as the solar and the lunar flows.
2.47ab When the breath flows through the lunar channel (candravāha), the yogi should practice retention (kumbhaka).
2.47cd By means of the lunar flow, he should fill his own body with air. 2.48ab Emission (utsarga) by means of the solar flow (ravivāha) is recommended for the growth of the body.
2.48cd Thus, O Goddess, has the fourfold station of the *kalā* been described to you.
2.49ab Hereafter, I shall proclaim the great state of supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*).
2.49cd The *vajrakanda*, located in the forehead, resembles a blazing moon.
2.50ab Within that square [mandala] containing the syllable *laṃ*, the supreme god Śiva resides.
2.50cd The deities and the yogins, united with their powers (*śakti*), worship him there.
2.51ab O Great Goddess, on the surface of the crest [of the head], it possesses a radiance equal to a hundred thousand suns.

2.51cd–2.52ab: In the center of the triangular maṇḍala, one should meditate upon the god Śiva in the form of a *liṅga*, O Goddess, as the supreme reality situated within the midst of the *raṅga* (the colored field), embraced by his own Śakti. 2.52cd:
O Supreme Lady, one should contemplate him as being attended by the hosts of deities.

O highly fortunate goddess, one should meditate upon the god Maheśvara there in the right conch-shell, which is endowed with a circle of six dots, contains the syllable *yaṃ*, and is smoke-colored; he is in the form of a *liṅga*, joined with Śakti, and surrounded by his attendants.
2.54cd In the left temple, O Śivā, is a mandala resembling a half-moon, together with a lotus. 2.55ab Within it, in the center, is a firm linga made of nectar, containing the syllable *vaṃ*.
2.55cd It has the appearance of white cow’s milk and the brilliance of ten thousand autumn moons.
2.56ab Endowed with its own power and served by hosts of deities;
2.56cd Thus, O Goddess, the locations in the four directions have indeed been described by me.
2.57ab In their midst, O Pārvatī, is the great circle (*mahāvṛtta*) containing the syllable *Haṃ*.

The Supreme Lord, the transcendent Śambhu, remains accompanied by his own power; he is in the form of the *liṅga*, joined by the Gaṇas, with a splendor equal to ten million suns. On the western forehead is the Lord of the Earth, the Leader of the Sun.
2.59ab The Lord of Wind is in the right temple; the Lord of Water is in the left;
Śambhu, the Lord of Space, is in the center. These five locations have been declared by me.
2.59cd–60ab Four finger-breadths above the head of the god who is the Lord of Space [is the location].
Situated in the center of the circle of light, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons,
it is a vessel consisting of divine nectar, with the root-lock as its door-panels;
it is the upward-facing moon, the great mountain, indivisible, and the abode of the Unchanging.
O Īśvarī, within the midst of cool nectar, the *liṅga* is dissolved;
it resembles a mote of dust, possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons,
is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, and dispels the darkness of ignorance.
Having transcended the five stages for the sake of perceiving the supreme reality, one should,
with the mind, extend the goddess Vāgīśī— who is the vessel for the jar of supreme nectar and possesses a door fitted with the *kumbhaka*— with her face turned upwards.
2.65ab The yogi, having restrained the movement of the vital breath, shall effortlessly open the bolt with the tongue. 2.65cd Having attained the Truth together with the mind,
[he finds] there the cool, nectar-like milk, sweet as sugarcane juice and cold.
2.66cd The yogi should drink the yogic draught, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. 2.67ab Satisfied by that nourishment of nectar and having attained the supreme state,
2.67cd and having achieved union with the *unmanī* [state] therein, within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
2.68ab The yogi should consume with yoga the flesh consisting of sound and the drop (nāda-bindu).
2.68cd O Mistress of the Gods, this secret has been proclaimed as difficult to attain.
2.69ab It was spoken by the omniscient Śiva; whatever fruit is found in the lineage of the scriptures [is obtained thereby].
2.69cd One truly obtains that fruit within six months; there is no doubt in this matter.

2.70ab O Goddess, he who, having attained the lineage of accomplishments (*siddhi-santāna*), does not understand this yoga— 2.70cd nothing at all should be told to him by one desiring accomplishment (*siddhi*).

2.71ab They do not know the Guru as God, nor likewise the commitments (samaya) declared in the scriptures. 2.71cd To those who are devoted to hypocrisy and crookedness, one should not impart the scripture.
2.72ab O Goddess, fire, consisting of all splendor, resides at the root of the tongue.
2.72cd The sun is at its tip, and the moon is established at the root of the palate.
2.73ab He who knows this according to reality attains accomplishment.
2.73cd Having churned the mandala of fire, one should awaken it with effort.

2.74ab Melted by its heat and essence, that lunar orb born of the palate should be taken up by the tongue presided over by the Sun. 2.74cd O Goddess, that supreme nectar, cool and dripping from the moon—
2.75cd One should collect with a vessel that which issues from the nostrils.
2.76ab By massaging the limbs with that, the purification of the channels truly arises.
2.76cd [One should likewise collect] the essence of the *cāmara* that has emerged from the anus and the genitals and has come out into a vessel.
Having stirred the nectar from the armpits and refined it with the juices of the lower lip,
the yogi, by performing bodily massage with that, becomes free from disease in this world;
he truly becomes strong and is devoid of wrinkles and grey hair.

2.78cd Having thoroughly rubbed the root of the tongue, one should rub one's own body with the great fluid produced there. 2.79ab First, by doing this for half a year, the tongue becomes four finger-breadths longer; of this there is no doubt. 2.79cd And it grows [further], there is no doubt in this matter.
2.80ab O Śivā, having drawn the tongue upward with the fingers of the right hand,
2.80cd and having struck the uvula with the fingers of the left hand, O Śivā,
2.81ab one should churn the seat of fire, turning it gradually upward.
2.81cd And above the Trikūṭa, within a portion of the moon, one should take refuge in the abode of Śiva.
2.82ab This Khecarīmudrā, which destroys death, has been described to you.
2.82cd Indeed, for one who is habituated to such practice, obstacles do arise.
2.83ab There are four types of *bhaṭas* and likewise four types of *naṭas*.
2.83cd Emaciation of the limbs, hunger, laziness, itching, and discoloration of the body— 2.84ab these are the symptoms of the *bhaṭa*; hear now their remedies.
2.84cd Having rendered the mind free from objects, for three months [one should use] the juice of the *amarī* plant.
2.85ab One should rub the body with that; thereby the growth of the body is produced.
2.85cd One should perform the rubbing three times each, both by day and likewise by night.
2.86ab Having directed the tongue upward toward the position of the *vajrakanda*,
2.86cd for one who licks that nectar, hunger and laziness truly perish.
2.87ab O Goddess, by taking that immortal nectar and massaging the limbs, [the body becomes supple].
2.87cd The discoloration of one's own body and itching also perish.
2.88ab And the four types of *naṭabhedas*, O beloved, exist in many ways;
2.88cd [the symptoms are] eye disease, trembling of the limbs, burning sensation, and likewise delusion.
2.89ab One variety has been declared by me; now hear the second.
2.89cd It is characterized by toothache, diminished vitality, and the loss of bodily lightness.
2.90ab Likewise, O Goddess, hear of the third variety, which is the great fever (mahājvara).
2.90cd Headache and the disorder of phlegm—let the fourth [disorder] be considered.
2.91ab Vomiting, the disorder of breathlessness (asthma), and likewise blindness of the eyes;
2.91cd And likewise, difficult-to-conquer sleep—for these, hear the remedy.
2.92ab One should lead Kuṇḍalinī, who is pierced by breath and accompanied by its root, upwards. 2.92cd Having made the tongue motionless and directed upwards, one should take recourse in *kumbhaka*.
2.93ab O Great Goddess, from the agitation of the Power (*śakti*), the Great Sound (*mahānāda*) arises.
2.93cd When he hears that sound, then he is said to be liberated.
2.94ab O Supreme Goddess, he should contemplate his own body as being sprinkled with nectar.
2.94cd By this, O Goddess, within one month he is released from previous defects.
If one should practice according to this very same procedure for two months, then one hears with both ears the sound of a great elephant trumpeting.
One should contemplate the body as before; by means of the second [set of mantras], one is liberated from diseases.
2.96cd After three months, by hearing the Brahmā-nāda, one should recollect it as before;
2.97ab One is liberated from the defects of the third division; there is no doubt in this.
2.97cd In the fourth monthly cycle, [one hears] the Meghanāda, known as Aghora.

2.98ab Having heard this and practiced as before, one is liberated from the defects of delusion. 2.98cd Thus, with a steady mind, one should practice meditation throughout the three periods of the day.
2.99ab One shall accomplish this within three years; indeed, truth arises, and one becomes free from old age and death.

2.99cd–2.100ab: Indeed, I have already declared the prevention of the four defects of the soldier as well as the defect of the actor; listen further, O Lord of the Gods, concerning the yogi who, in this peaceful and supreme reality, is established in yoga characterized by bliss.
2.100cd: [He is] that yogi who, in this peaceful and supreme reality, is established in yoga characterized by bliss.
2.101ab I bow at the feet of him who has entered [the state] and knows all principles.
2.101cd O Goddess, the first is movement, and the second would be piercing (bhedana). 2.102ab The third is praised as churning (mathana), and the fourth is entry (praveśana).
2.102cd Having pulled up the root of the palate, O beloved, one should draw the tongue upward. 2.103ab One should know that movement as the "breaking of the bolt of Brahman" (brahmārgalavibhedana).
2.103cd They call that breaking "churning" (mathana) by means of the thread (tantu), O beloved.

2.104ab When one performs churning by means of inserting an iron nail, 2.104cd one should know that churning, O beloved, brings about the increase of yoga. 2.105ab Having opened the bolt, one should extend the tongue upward into the sky.
2.105cd They call the entry [into the center], O Sovereign Goddess, that which sets in motion the perfection of yoga.
2.106ab By means of breaking through the bolt of Brahmā and by the shifting of the tongue, 2.106cd a realization arises instantly, O Supreme Sovereign; this is the truth.
2.107ab At first there is a state of bliss, and after that, the loss of sleep; 2.107cd union and eating occur only in very small measure. 2.108ab Nourishment arises and vitality increases, O beloved.

2.108cd There is neither old age nor death, nor disease, nor gray hair; 2.109ab O Great Goddess, he becomes one whose vital energy flows upward (ūrdhvaretas), endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, 2.109cd if he should thus accomplish yoga with an unwavering state of being.
2.110ab O Pārvatī, at that time one correctly obtains these aforementioned fruits.
2.110cd O Goddess worshipped by heroes, Śrī and Vāgīśā are established on the tip of the tongue.
2.111ab In the region of the root of the tongue, which serves as its support, death through bondage is established.
O Mother of the Gaṇas, uproot everything that constitutes the state of bondage and death.
O Moon, one should enter through its tip into the abode known as Śrīśambhu.
O Goddess, by means of this yoga and with the mind firmly established therein—
2.113ab The yogi enters the state of absorption into Unmanī; he attains dissolution therein.
2.113cd The realization of that dissolution arises immediately, without deliberation.
2.114ab Having fixed the mind on the tip of the tongue, one should perceive that effulgence with the eyes.
2.114cd–115ab: From the *mūlādhāra*, one should lead the vital breath upward through the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
Having reached the abode of Brahmā, the yogi should fix the mind in the void. 2.115cd:
In this way, he should meditate upon the supreme reality, which is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted.
2.116ab The celestial Gaṅgā flows from the abode of Brahmā, exceedingly cool. 2.116cd By drinking it for only a month, one will certainly become possessed of a vajra-body.
2.117ab One will truly possess a divine body, divine speech, and divine vision.

O Goddess, one shall possess divine intellect and likewise divine hearing. One should contemplate Vāgīśā, who has the luster of ten million moons upon the tip of the tongue and is satiated by the essence of supreme nectar; thus, one attains poetic genius in an instant.
2.119ab Meditating on Lakṣmī, who resides at the tip of the tongue and is delighted by supreme nectar, 2.119cd the yogi, O Maheśānī, shall attain the sovereignty of yoga.
2.120ab Five innate [powers] are renowned within this body, which is of the nature of the Supreme Self.
2.120cd When the body is produced within the mother’s body from the dissolution of the father, 2.121ab there, as that body attains growth, it exists together with [the following]:
2.121cd The primordial Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is remembered as the first innate [power].
The second is called Suṣumṇā, and the tongue is indeed the third;
the fourth is the location of the palate, while the fifth is the location of Brahmā.
Having raised the first innate [power], one should place the second innate [power] there.
2.123cd One should enter the third *sahaja* above the fourth *sahaja*.
2.124ab Having pierced the fourth *sahaja*, one should enter the fifth *sahaja*. 2.124cd This division has been proclaimed by me; it is difficult to discern, O Mistress of the Kula.
3.1ab From the root, the Kuṇḍalinī energy has entered the path of the Suṣumṇā;
3.1cd resembling a single strand of spider-silk, it possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
3.2ab Having entered the path of the uvula (ghaṇṭikā), [it reaches] the bolt of the door of Śiva in Śivā.
3.2cd Having pierced [the path] with the tongue and by means of *kumbhaka*, O Maheśvarī,
3.3ab the yogin should enter the self-existent abode (*svāyaṃbhuvam dhāma*), which shines like ten million suns, O beloved; 3.3cd there, in that great ocean of nectar characterized by cool waves,
3.4ab Having drunk the nectar and rested with an intellect filled with supreme bliss, 3.4cd one should contemplate one's own body as satiated by that nectar.
3.5ab Through this divine yoga, divine vision arises.
3.5cd True flight through the sky shall come to pass, as well as the destruction of all diseases. 3.6ab There shall be evasion of timely death, as well as wandering through the three worlds.
3.6cd Endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he will certainly become a perfected being (saṃsiddha).

3.7ab He attains the state of a lord of yogins, and his movement becomes unimpeded. 3.7cd Endowed himself with the strength of nine thousand elephants, 3.8ab he is born like Śiva, O Goddess; this which I have spoken is the truth, the absolute truth.

3.8cd Between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, the *suṣumṇā* exists in the form of light. 3.9ab Therein resides the stainless radiance, devoid of color, form, and qualities. 3.9cd That which is like a slumbering serpent is the supreme *kuṇḍalinī*.
3.10ab The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Ṛt [are] known as Iḍā and Piṅgalā.
3.10cd One should place that Śakti between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. 3.11ab O Śivā, one should establish her, whose form is supreme nectar, reaching as far as the abode of Brahmā.
3.11cd Truly, one becomes absorbed in that [reality], oneself becoming eternally of the nature of nectar.
3.12ab The Power (Śakti), having reached the abode of Śiva, attains the supreme state from the Supreme Lord.
3.12cd Fully satisfied by the gratification of that enjoyment, she is filled with supreme bliss.
3.13ab Sprinkling the body of the yogin from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, 3.13cd with nectar that is cool, unctuous, and refreshing, O Supreme Goddess;
3.14ab it then returns to its own abode by that very same path, O Auspicious One.
3.14cd This secret yoga has been declared, O you who are worshipped by the lords of yogis.

3.15ab Having cast aside all scriptures and whatever ritual acts such as recitation and fire-offerings there may be, 3.15cd the yogi, liberated from both merit and demerit, should practice yoga thoroughly.
3.16ab Having made the tongue upward-pointing, one should place it upon the Trikūṭa.
3.16cd [This is] in the Brahmāṇḍa, below the Brahma-line, in the orb above the rājadanta.
3.17ab One should know that to be the Trikūṭa; therein is the brilliantly radiant Liṅga.
3.17cd Released from the sequence of time, it is difficult to discern even for the gods.
3.18ab Night is declared to be in the *iḍā*, and day is remembered as being in the *piṅgalā*.
3.18cd O Goddess, the Moon and the Sun are eternally situated there, consisting of night and day.
3.19ab One should not worship the *liṅga* by day, nor by night, O Maheśvarī.
3.19cd One should always worship the *liṅga*, transcending the constraints of day and night.
3.20ab For this [universe] consists of day and night, born of the nature of the succession of time.
3.20cd By the cessation of the sequence of time, there shall be victory over death in time. 3.21ab One should contemplate one's own body as liberated from the sequence of time.
3.21cd One should worship it with the flower of meditative absorption and satisfy it with the nectar of the lotus.
3.22ab Thus, by the practice for six months, one indeed becomes free from old age and death.
3.22cd One attains omniscience, truly equal to Śiva, and free from all affliction.
3.23ab Having placed the tongue at the root of the palate, directed upward toward the face...
Having drunk the nectar produced there, the yogi should slowly, with a whistling sound (*śītkāra*),
drink the vital air (*pavana*) while established in the supportless, auspicious state;
having joined the mind with the *unmanī* state, he should practice the innate yoga (*sahajayoga*).
3.25ab By this yoga, indeed, within six months the practitioner becomes free from old age and death.
3.25cd O Goddess, one should join the chin to the circle of the sixteen vowels.
3.26ab Having fixed the eyes between the eyebrows, one should extend the tongue upward.
Having attained the state of *kumbhaka* by blocking the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*,
and having awakened the root power (*mūlaśakti*), one pierces the six lotuses within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*),
which resembles a thousand flashes of lightning.
3.28ab Having settled [the mind] for a long time in the abode, the cool ocean of nectar, one shall dwell there.
3.28cd When the yogi dwells at ease in the abode consisting of Brahman,
3.29ab then, as if the body were lifeless, that state shines forth as a radiance within it.
3.29cd By this yoga, O Goddess, one should practice for seven days;
3.30ab whenever that occurs, he becomes free from old age and death.
3.30cd By practicing for only a month, one may live as long as the moon and stars endure.
3.31 When the yogi, having effortlessly pierced the city of Brahmā,
proceeds [further], O Śivā, he then attains the state of Śiva, consisting of an eternal body. 3.32 He shall never again drink from a mother’s breast within the wheel of saṃsāra.

3.32cd But when the intellect of the yogin becomes intent on leaving this body, 3.33ab then, having become firm in posture, the knower of the Self should for a long time contemplate the root-power (mūlaśakti),
which is brilliantly radiant and resembles ten million suns. 3.33cd He, the knower of the Self, should meditate upon it for a long duration.
3.34ab Having withdrawn one's own life-force, which extends down to the soles of the feet,
by means of a gradual process, one should lead it to the station of the *mūlādhāra*.
3.35ab Therein [resides] the power of Kuṇḍalinī, resembling the fire of universal destruction (*saṃvarta*).
3.35cd One should indeed contemplate with the intellect [the power] devouring the vital breath, the wind, and the senses.

3.36ab Having reached the state of *kumbhaka* (retention), radiant as a circle of lightning, 3.36cd O Goddess of Gods, having drawn it up from the root, one should lead it to the station of *svādhiṣṭhāna*.

3.37ab There, the practitioner should meditate on her swallowing the entire individual soul (jīva) situated therein. 3.37cd Having quickly drawn [the soul] upward from there, resembling ten million flashes of lightning,
3.38ab and having reached the station of Maṇipūra, he should perform [the practice] there as before.
3.38cd Having raised [the breath] from that again, one should lead it to the station of Anāhata.
3.39ab Having remained there for a moment, O Goddess, one should indeed remember Satī as before.
3.39cd And having raised it once more, one should cause it to enter the sixteen-spoked lotus.
3.40ab There too, O Goddess, the knower of the path of yoga should contemplate as before.
3.40cd Having drawn [the vital breath] up from there and led the life-force (*jīva*) to the space between the eyebrows, one should swallow it again.
3.41ab [One should contemplate] the Great Power (*mahāśakti*), who has swallowed the life-force and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
3.41cd Together with the mind, Vāgīśī, having in an instant burst open the bolt of Brahman,
3.42ab Should properly take rest in the great ocean of supreme nectar (parāmṛta).
3.42cd O Goddess, the Supreme Śiva, the ultimate cause, resides there.
3.43ab Having united [the breath] with the power (*śakti*), one should contemplate the unity of those two.
3.43cd If one who knows the divisions of time is intent on deceiving Time,
3.44ab then for as long as that time passes, one should dwell there in happiness.
3.44cd Below the bolt of the door of Brahman lies the purpose of the body and time.
3.45ab Therefore, O Goddess, in the state above that, there is indeed no purpose for time.
3.45cd When the Goddess perceives that her own time has passed, [she acts].
3.46ab Then, having broken through the bolt of Brahmā, one should lead the Śakti to the root-plane (mūlapada).
3.46cd One should likewise lead the individual soul (svajīva), born from the body of the Śakti, together with the sense organs.
3.47ab Having joined it to its respective activity, one may dwell happily with a healthy body.
3.47cd By this yoga, O Goddess, one may deceive even the arrived time of death. 3.48ab If the desire to cast off the human body arises,
3.48cd then, being supremely satisfied, [one beholds] Śiva who has reached the station of Brahmā.

3.49ab Having joined with his power and pierced through the sky, he should enter the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā). 3.49cd He should enter the element of space (vyomatattva) into the great void (mahāvyoman), and the element of air (vāyutattva) into the great wind (mahānila). 3.50ab He should enter the element of fire (tejastattva) into the great fire (mahātejas), and the element of water (aptattva) into the sphere of water (jalamaṇḍala).
3.50cd One should place the earth-element in the portion of the earth, and the mind in the groundless state (pada).
3.51ab One should settle one's own senses within the elements whose qualities are space and so forth.
3.51cd Thus, having abandoned that which pertains to saṃsāra, one relies upon the supreme reality.

3.52ab Untouched by the five elements and the rest, having pierced the orb of the sun, 3.52cd merged into the peaceful and auspicious state of the supreme reality (paratattva), he becomes Śiva himself. 3.53ab There shall be no returning again for thousands of millions of kalpas.
3.53cd If he does not cast off his body for the sake of favoring the worlds,
3.54ab then, at the end of the dissolution, having abandoned the physical form, he remains established in his own self.
3.54cd Thus, this is the Khecarīmudrā, which bestows the sovereignty of the Lord of the Sky-farers (Khecarīs).
3.55ab This [knowledge] destroys birth, death, old age, disease, wrinkles, and grey hair.

3.55cd Indeed, there is no science (*vidyā*) like this anywhere in any other scripture. 3.56ab O Goddess, one should not reveal the secret union with the Sky-farer (*khecarī*), which is well-guarded as a profound secret.
3.56cd And this practice of its cultivation has been revealed to you out of affection.
3.57ab O Goddess, she who is named Khecarī is worshipped by all the lords of yogins; 3.57cd O Śivā, he who does not know her in this world is called a beast.
3.58ab For one who is constantly habituated to practice, even while wandering through the three worlds,
3.58cd and for one who practices the knowledge obtained from the mouth of the Guru,
3.59ab and whose mind is perpetually attached to the *khecarīmelaka* and other [yogic unions].
3.59cd Without my propitiation, the great yoga is not accomplished.
3.60ab For those devoid of my grace, whose minds are intent on reviling me,
3.60cd for those bound by the fetters of the bound (paśu), yoga results only in affliction.
3.61ab Abandoning the worship taught by the omniscient Śiva, my own,
3.61cd for one who constantly practices [other forms], O Goddess, yoga leads only to destruction.
3.62ab O Goddess, one should satisfy with devotion Śiva, who consists of all the worlds.
3.62cd But for one whose mind is attached to me alone, all the deities are pleased.

3.63ab Therefore, having worshipped me, one should practice the flight through the sky (khe-carī) by my grace. 3.63cd Otherwise, there will be only suffering; there is no accomplishment even in ten million births.

3.64ab O Supreme Goddess, all mantras and yogas are perfected for one who is habituated to my worship and whose mind is attached solely to me. 3.64cd–3.65ab Therefore, O Goddess, one should worship me for the sake of the increase of all yoga.
3.65cd Delighted by the Khecarī [mudrā], the yogi should practice yoga that is absorbed in That.
3.66ab In a solitary place, free from living beings and devoid of all disturbances, 3.66cd Equipped with all the necessary means and free from all worldly thoughts.
3.67ab Having taken his seat on a soft cushion according to the method taught by his own guru, 3.67cd he should perform each practice one by one, relying upon the words of the guru.
3.68ab This yoga has been described by me; it is the accomplisher of all yogas.
3.68cd Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, what more do you wish to hear?
3.69ab O Śambhu, victory to you who are adorned with the crescent moon and attainable through true devotion!
3.69cd By you, the secret Śrīkhecarī-vidyā has been excellently explained.
4.1ab Now I shall fully explain to you the most divine medicinal herbs;

4.1cd without such herbs, a yogin will never attain accomplishment. 4.2ab [The powder] made from the leaves, flowers, fruits, stalks, and roots of that plant named after the head of the supreme mendicant (Śiva).

4.2cd One should administer the meat-broths separately with buttermilk, sour gruel, milk, honey, sugar, and so forth; this will effectively eliminate greying hair, bestow great strength, noble virility, energy, and the removal of diseases.

4.3ab A boar [is said to have] ears, Garuḍa eyes, and claws and teeth equal to adamant. 4.3cd Possessing the speed equal to the great wind, such a youth shall live as long as the earth, the moon, and the stars.

4.4ab One should consume the powder of *vārāhī* root together with ghee and jaggery for nourishment and growth; with buttermilk (*takra*), there is destruction of hemorrhoids (*durnāman*); furthermore, with cow’s milk, there is destruction of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). 4.4cd One should cause that powder to be drunk twice daily with sugar and other substances, as well as honey and milk; for two years, one becomes black-haired, with wrinkles and grey hair destroyed, and capable of splitting black stones with the body. 4.5ab [One should take] *guggulu* combined with castor oil and *triphalā*.
4.5cd The wise man should consume sulphur, which destroys old age and poverty.
4.6ab Aśvagandhā, sesame seeds, black gram, sugar, and Viśvasarpikā—
4.6cd By using these for just one month, neither disease nor death shall occur.
4.7ab O beloved, immortality is attained within five months by means of these five [substances].
4.7cd One should consume sulphur, triphalā, and kuṣṭha, combined with the three sweetening agents (madhuratrika).
4.8ab Rising in the morning, one should eat this; after six months, it destroys wrinkles and grey hair.
4.8cd O Goddess, mercury, sulfur, orpiment, and realgar; 4.9ab *kunaṣṭikā*, the powder of *yaṣṭi*, the substance called *rudra*, and the powder of *muṇḍikā*;
4.9cd having tasted these saturated with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*) within a year.
4.10ab Having dried the *bhṛṅga* plant together with its roots, one should prepare a powder of black sesame seeds and *āmalaka* in half that quantity.

4.10cd By regularly tasting this with the three kinds of honey for a year, there will be no diseases, nor old age, nor death. 4.11ab One should consume each leaf of *nirguṇḍī* at the three times of day.
4.11cd O Goddess, in twelve years one shall become free from old age and death.
4.12ab One should prepare an equal quantity of the powder of *nirguṇḍī*, *malamūṇḍī*, and [other herbs]. 4.12cd Taken with sugar, ghee, and honey, after one year it destroys wrinkles and grey hair.
4.13ab One *māṣaka* each of sulfur, gold, *tālaka*, and *rudralocana* [taken] for a year,
combined with the three sweets, bestows freedom from old age and death.
4.14ab Mercury, the exudate of the *śālmali* tree, and sulfur, [taken] with the three sweets...
Having risen in the morning, one should consume it; after six months, one becomes free from old age and death.
